archival_memory.morning: I usually wake up around 6:30 in the morning. It's become a habit ever since I started wanting to get a head start on projects—though some days, especially if I was up late coding or gaming, I might sneak in an extra 15 minutes or so. The first thing I do is check my calendar on my phone, just to get my head around what's coming up that day. Then I do some basic stretching right there beside my bed, so I'm not half-asleep when I jump in the shower. I've found that if I skip the stretches, I'm sluggish for at least an hour or so, and let's be honest—who has time for that?

archival_memory.night: At night, I usually wind down by doing some light stretching or meditation. It helps me relax and clear my mind. I also make sure to set my alarm for the next day and get everything ready for the morning. It's a small task, but it helps me feel prepared and in control. After that, I can finally get some rest and do it all again the next day.

Usually, we're all hustling to get out the door. If I'm feeling ambitious, I'll whip up some scrambled eggs and spinach, maybe have a piece of whole wheat toast, and brew coffee using one of those single-cup machines we all share. If I'm rushed, I'll just grab a granola bar and some fruit to eat while I head to campus. I try to be economical with time while making sure I eat something relatively nutritious. I'm pretty active, so I can't slack on breakfast too often.

archival_memory.campus: Once I get to campus, I usually find a seat in the student center or a quiet corner of the library to finalize any small tasks—maybe a last-minute tweak to code for a morning lab or adjusting my to-do list for the day. I use a digital task manager that syncs across my devices, so I can reference it whenever. Having all my tasks in one place forces me to stay organized. I categorize tasks by class or project, and I try to break them down into smaller subtasks with clear deadlines. It helps me avoid feeling overwhelmed by big deadlines looming weeks away.
archival_memory.lunch: Class time itself usually extends until around 2:00 P.M. or 3:00 P.M., with a midday break in between. I'll grab a quick lunch on campus—my go-to is often a turkey and avocado wrap from one of the campus bistros. While I eat, I tend to check email and Slack messages from my research group, where I'm helping develop a computer vision application for analyzing images of marine traffic. My professor likes to set weekly milestones, so I need to constantly keep track of where we are in the cycle. On top of that, I'm part of a programming club that does hackathon prep, and they also often post about upcoming events or workshops. Staying on top of all these alerts is critical, or I'll miss something important.
archival_memory.weekends: On weekends, time management looks a bit different. Saturdays might be partially dedicated to longer assignments or bigger project milestones. But I also make space for fun stuff—maybe a sailing trip if the weather’s nice, or hanging out at a friend’s place for a casual gathering. Sundays, I attend a group study session with seven other classmates to prep for the week ahead. That’s where we catch up on each other’s workload and share tips or resources. Sometimes, I even go over internship or job application things on Sunday, just to keep everything in check for post-graduation planning.
archival_memory.productivity: If there’s one main strategy I’d recommend to anyone, it’s to keep a single, unified to-do list and calendar that reflect your actual priorities. For me, it’s a digital solution because I can’t carry a planner everywhere, but some people do well with bullet journals. As long as you know where you stand on assignments, projects, or personal goals, you’ll feel more in control. Also, don’t forget to schedule downtime. It sounds counterintuitive, but letting your brain breathe helps you come back stronger and more productive. Even if it’s just an hour at the end of the day to watch a show or play with your dog, it matters.
